title: Is There a Money-Making Loop
statement:
A directed graph has `n` nodes (`0` to `n - 1`). `edges[i] = [from, to, weight]` is a directed edge; the weight may be **negative**. A **cycle** is a path that starts and ends at the same node (a self-loop `[v, v, w]` is a cycle of one edge). Its weight is the sum of the weights of its edges.

Return `true` if the graph contains a cycle whose total weight is **negative** (less than 0), anywhere in the graph, otherwise `false`. A cycle of weight exactly `0` does not count.

examples.explanation: The same loop has weight 0, which is not negative.

hints.nudge: Imagine you keep improving the shortest-distance estimates by following edges. In a graph without a negative cycle, how many rounds of improvement can there be at most? What happens if there is one?
hints.pattern: Bellman-Ford: start every distance at 0 (so every component is covered), relax all edges up to n times; if the distances still change in round n, a negative cycle exists.
hints.pseudocode:
dist = [0] * n
repeat n times:
  changed = false
  for (u, v, w) in edges: if dist[u] + w < dist[v]: dist[v] = dist[u] + w; changed = true
  if not changed: return false
return true
hints.walkthrough: Checking all cycles is exponential. The estimates dist[v] only ever go down. Without a negative cycle, a shortest path uses at most n - 1 edges, so after n - 1 rounds of 'relax every edge' nothing can improve any more, and round n changes nothing. With a negative cycle you can keep going around it and lowering the distances for ever, so the distances still change in every round. Starting all distances at 0 is like adding a hidden start node that has a zero-weight edge to every node: it makes cycles in any part of the graph reachable, even in nodes that are not connected to node 0. So run the rounds; if a round changes nothing, answer false; if all n rounds changed something, answer true. Floyd-Warshall gives the same answer (a negative number on the diagonal) in O(n^3).
